title: HS256 by hand
summary: Sign and verify a JWT with HMAC-SHA256 using nothing but the base class library.

steps.title: HMAC: a hash with a key
body: **HS256** means *HMAC with SHA-256*. HMAC (RFC 2104) mixes a secret key into a hash, so only someone who knows the key can produce the right output:
```csharp fragment
byte[] mac = HMACSHA256.HashData(key, message);   // 32 bytes
A JWT's signature is the HMAC of the ASCII text `base64url(header) + "." + base64url(payload)`, called the **signing input**, then base64url-encoded:
```text
signature = base64url( HMAC-SHA256( secret, "eyJhbGci...J9.eyJzdWIi...fQ" ) )

The same secret signs and verifies, which makes HS256 **symmetric**. That is simple and fast, and fine when one service both issues and checks its own tokens. Its limits are the subject of the next lesson.
The secret must be **random and at least 256 bits** (32 bytes), for example `RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes(32)`. A word like `"secret"` can be guessed offline from any one token.

steps.explain: 32 bytes encode to 43 base64url characters (44 with padding). Changing a single bit of the key gives a completely different MAC.

steps.title: Signing, step by step
body: Building a token is four lines. Step through it:
The output is a perfectly ordinary HS256 JWT. Paste it into any JWT debugger with the key and it verifies.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines that create an HS256 token.
steps.explain: Encode both JSON parts, join them with a dot, MAC the joined text, append the encoded MAC.

steps.title: Verifying
body: Verification recomputes the MAC and compares:
```csharp fragment
var parts = token.Split('.');
if (parts.Length != 3) return false;
// 1. Which algorithm does the header claim? Only accept the one you expect.
using var header = JsonDocument.Parse(FromB64Url(parts[0]));
if (header.RootElement.GetProperty("alg").GetString() != "HS256") return false;
// 2. Recompute over the parts exactly as received, and compare in constant time.
byte[] expected = HMACSHA256.HashData(secret, Encoding.ASCII.GetBytes(parts[0] + "." + parts[1]));
return CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals(expected, FromB64Url(parts[2]));
Two details matter:
- MAC the parts **as received**. Don't decode and re-encode the JSON first: a different spacing or key order changes the bytes.
- Compare with `FixedTimeEquals`. An early-exit comparison lets an attacker discover a valid signature byte by byte (the timing attack from the foundations module).
A valid signature proves the token came from someone holding the secret and wasn't modified. It does **not** prove the token is still valid: `exp`, `iss` and `aud` are checked afterwards.

steps.prompt: Why must the signature be recomputed over the base64url parts exactly as they arrived?
options: Re-encoding the decoded JSON can change the bytes (spacing, key order, escaping), so a genuine token would fail
To make verification slower for attackers
It doesn't matter; any equivalent JSON gives the same signature
steps.explain: The signature covers bytes, not meaning. `{"a":1}` and `{ "a": 1 }` are equal JSON with different signatures.
The MAC covers header and payload, and the received signature (part 2) is decoded before the constant-time compare.

steps.prompt: Ada edits her token's payload to say `admin`, keeping the original signature. What does this print?
steps.explain: Without the secret Ada can't compute the matching signature for her edited payload, so the server rejects it. (Real code compares with `FixedTimeEquals`; `==` keeps this example short.)

steps.title: Sign and verify HS256
prompt: - `string CreateHs256(string payloadJson, byte[] secret)`: the header is exactly `{"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}`.

- `bool VerifyHs256(string token, byte[] secret)`: `true` only when the token has three parts, its header's `alg` is `"HS256"`, and the signature matches (constant-time). Return `false`, never throw, for garbage input.
The tests import `System.Security.Cryptography` and `System.Text.Json`. With the secret `dojo-secret` and the payload `{"sub":"ada","name":"Ada Lovelace","iat":1700000000}`, your token must be:
solution: case 1: throw new FormatException("Not valid base64url.");
if (!header.RootElement.TryGetProperty("alg", out var alg) || alg.GetString() != "HS256") return false;
catch (Exception e) when (e is FormatException or JsonException)
hints: Sign: encode header and payload, join with `.`, `HMACSHA256.HashData(secret, Encoding.ASCII.GetBytes(input))`, append.
Verify: split, check `alg` in the decoded header, recompute, `CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals`.
Wrap the decoding in `try { ... } catch (Exception e) when (e is FormatException or JsonException) { return false; }`.
template: Dojo.Eq("CreateHs256 makes the exact sample token", "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJhZGEiLCJuYW1lIjoiQWRhIExvdmVsYWNlIiwiaWF0IjoxNzAwMDAwMDAwfQ.Cm2LgthmpjCZHddLllEQKSLKKh8papMu4017Z39uMwE", dojoTok);
Dojo.Eq("VerifyHs256 accepts it", true, VerifyHs256(dojoTok, dojoSecret));
Dojo.Eq("a different secret is rejected", false, VerifyHs256(dojoTok, System.Text.Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("dojo-secreT")));
Dojo.Eq("a tampered payload is rejected", false, VerifyHs256(DojoJwt.Tamper(dojoTok), dojoSecret));
Dojo.Eq("a token from the tests' own signer is accepted", true, VerifyHs256(DojoJwt.Hs("{\"sub\":\"grace\"}", dojoSecret), dojoSecret));
Dojo.Eq("alg HS512 in the header is rejected", false, VerifyHs256(DojoJwt.Hs("{\"alg\":\"HS512\"}", "{\"sub\":\"ada\"}", dojoSecret), dojoSecret));
Dojo.Eq("alg none with an empty signature is rejected", false, VerifyHs256("eyJhbGciOiJub25lIn0.eyJzdWIiOiJhZG1pbiJ9.", dojoSecret));
Dojo.Eq("garbage is rejected without throwing", false, VerifyHs256("not.a.jwt!", dojoSecret));
Dojo.Eq("two parts are rejected", false, VerifyHs256("abc.def", dojoSecret));
